The Dancing Shiva, also known as Nataraja, is a depiction of the Hindu god Shiva as the cosmic dancer who performs his divine dance to destroy a weary universe and then recreate it. This iconographic form of Shiva is most often associated with the Chola dynasty of Tamil Nadu, India, and became a symbol of royalty in that region. The dancing Shiva became a part of Chola era processions and religious festivals, a practice that continued thereafter.

The depiction of the dancing Shiva is often shown with specific items, including a drum (mudra) in his upper right hand, fire (agni) in his lower right hand, his raised left leg (or in rare cases, the right leg) representing liberation, and his lowered left hand (abhaya mudra) granting protection. His body, fingers, ankles, neck, face, head, ear lobes, and dress are shown decorated with symbolic items, which vary with historic period and region. He is surrounded by a ring of flames, standing on a lotus pedestal, lifting his left leg (or in rare cases, the right leg) and balancing / trampling upon a demon shown as a dwarf (Apasmara).

The dancing Shiva is also depicted in various postures, including the Urdhva Tandava, which is the dance of bliss, and the Lasya, which is the gentle dance. In Nepal, Assam, and Bengal, the dancing Shiva is sometimes shown as dancing on his vahana (animal vehicle) Nandi, the bull, and is regionally known as Narteshvara.

The depiction of the dancing Shiva has been informed of cosmic or metaphysical connotations, and is also argued on the basis of the testimony of the hymns of Tamil saints.
